1:
The chapter opens not with the customary formula but with an unusual notice — the inhabitants of Jerusalem themselves made Ahaziah king — and the witnesses read that irregularity closely. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that where the older record simply says, at 2 Kings 8:24, "and Ahaziah his son was king in his stead," the Chronicle gives fuller information, and that the very verb "they made king" carries a hint that the succession was disputed or doubtful; for where a son follows his father without opposition, the Chronicle too says only "his son was king in his stead." The one person who could contest the throne, they add, was his mother Athaliah, who would seize it after his death — the shadow of v.10 already falling across the accession.

Charles Ellicott, his fellow grammatical-historical witness, weighs the same anomaly but leans the other way. The departure from the usual "and Ahaziah his son reigned in his stead" has been supposed to mark a disputed succession, whether Athaliah the queen-mother or Jehoiada the high priest opposing it; but he judges it more likely that the difference of expression simply points to the writer's use of a different source. He fills in the raiders behind the slaughter: "the band that came with the Arabians to the camp" was some party of half-savage warriors who, after the Jewish camp had been stormed and the royal princes taken prisoner, fell upon and slew their captives, a scene he compares with Judges 8:18 and 1 Samuel 15:32; and "all the eldest" he renders literally "the former."

Behind the accession, then, lies a massacre. The reformed John Gill marks that Ahaziah was the sole surviving son, spared when all the rest were carried off and killed — the same lone survivor met at the close of the previous chapter in 2 Chron. 21:17. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the thing plainly, that all the others had been slain by the Arabians, and sketches in advance the whole arc of the reign: Ahaziah reigning wickedly under his mother's counsel, cut off by Jehu who destroys the house of Ahab, and Athaliah then destroying the seed royal but for the one child hidden in the temple. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the moral frame the bare verse implies — here begins the short and ruinous reign in which the counsel of the ungodly destroys a young prince, and a wicked woman labours to extinguish the house of David; yet, as the chapter will show, no word of God shall fall to the ground, and the crown is preserved on the head of a single infant.
2:
"Forty and two years old was Ahaziah when he began to reign" — and the number is impossible, so the witnesses gather with one voice to correct it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the difficulty at its sharpest: Ahaziah could have been twenty-two, as 2 Kings 8:26 has it, but he could not have been forty-two without being two years older than his own father, who died at forty. The Syriac and Arabic read twenty-two, and some copies of the Septuagint twenty; the slip is easy, he explains, since in the old lettering the mem that stands for forty and the caph that stands for twenty are readily confounded, the more so in the ancient Samaritan characters. Both readings cannot be true, and he will have no forced reconciliation of a figure that makes the son older than the father — "Apage hae nugae!"

The grammatical-historical witnesses reason to the same end more quietly. Keil and Delitzsch call forty-two an orthographical error for twenty-two, the beth having been changed into a mem; since Joram was thirty-two at his accession and reigned eight years, his youngest son could be no older than twenty-one or twenty-two, Joram having begotten him about his eighteenth or nineteenth year — wholly possible in the East, where marriage came early and the princes had several wives. Charles Ellicott agrees it is an error of transcription, supported by the versions, and turns to the mother: "Athaliah the daughter of Omri" means his granddaughter, she being the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, and he notes that where Kings adds "king of Israel" the chronicler purposely omits it, as if to keep the taint of Omri's house at arm's length, in the spirit of Micah 6:16. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the manuscript evidence: the numeral letters for twenty-two and forty-two are easily mistaken, and the true reading survives in other Hebrew copies, in ancient Greek copies, and in the Syriac and Arabic — particularly, he says, in that most ancient Syriac copy long kept by the church of Antioch. "The daughter," he grants with the others, is here a granddaughter, for grandchildren are often called sons and daughters.

The reformed John Gill, weighing the same solutions, holds twenty-two to be undoubtedly the correct figure; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, though he too inclines to a transcriber's slip — noting that few books are printed without their errata — records the other guess that some have made, that "the son of forty-two years" means the son of a mother who was of that age, Athaliah's years being justly put for his own in reproach, since she managed him and in effect reigned while he held little more than the title of king.
3:
"He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly." The witnesses fasten on that second clause, which the chronicler alone supplies, and read the whole apostasy back to the woman who bred it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the emphasis of the opening pronoun — he too, like his father before him — where Kings had written only "and he walked"; and he notes that "his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly" is an explanatory remark added by the chronicler, not found in the parallel. Her influence, he judges, would be thrown behind the Baal-worship that was the very symbol of alliance with the northern kingdom, so that the king's private household piety and the kingdom's foreign policy corrupted together.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch reads the sentence the same way, as an accounting for the sin: he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, as his father Joram had done before him at 2 Chron. 21:6, precisely because his mother — a daughter of Ahab and the godless Jezebel — was his counsellor to do evil, leading him to give himself over to the idolatry of Ahab's house. The evil is not merely inherited but actively taught; the throne has a tutor, and she is Jezebel's daughter.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the portrait of that counsellor in a single stroke: Athaliah was the wicked daughter of a wicked parent and the wicked spouse of an unprincipled king, and every relation she stood in was a channel of corruption. The reformed John Gill, briefer still, simply binds the son's course to the father's — he walked in Ahab's ways as his father Jehoram had — so that the reader feels the momentum of two generations sliding the same way. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the chronicler's added clause and its political edge; Keil grounds the sin in the mother's tutelage; Clarke names her lineage of wickedness; Gill marks the unbroken descent from father to son. Between them they show that the calf- and Baal-worship of Samaria had now a settled advocate at the very heart of the Judean court, and that the young king's wickedness was less a personal choice than the harvest of a marriage his grandfather Jehoshaphat had made and his father Jehoram had deepened — the daughter of Ahab, planted in Jerusalem, teaching a king of David's line to walk after Ahab.
4:
"Wherefore he did evil in the sight of the LORD like the house of Ahab, for they were his counsellors after the death of his father to his destruction." The witnesses read the verse as the chronicler's own diagnosis of a ruin already set in motion. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that where 2 Kings 8:27 gives only the king's relationship to Ahab's house as the reason for his evil-doing, the Chronicle adds that its members — kin to him through his mother — became his counsellors after his father's death, and counsellors to his destruction, an expression they compare with 2 Chron. 20:23. How far that counsel led to his ruin is told in the verses that follow, which open with "he walked also in their counsel": it was on the advice of Ahab's relations that Ahaziah joined Joram in the very war that would bring the house of Ahab down and cost him his own life at v.5.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the wording. "To his destruction" is literally "to destruction to him," the same peculiar phrase that appeared at 2 Chron. 20:23; and this whole second half of the verse, he judges, is the chronicler's own free expansion and interpretation of the bare words of Kings, "for he was son-in-law of the house of Ahab." What Kings states as a fact of kinship the chronicler unfolds as a moral process — the kinship became a school of counsel, and the counsel became a snare.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the one distinction the verse quietly makes by its phrase "after the death of his father." While Jehoram lived, Wesley observes, the father himself seduced his son and made other evil counsellors unnecessary; only when he was gone did the house of Ahab close in to keep the young king firmly in the idolatry his father had begun in him. The reformed John Gill simply refers the reader back to the sentence already passed on the house of Ahab, letting the recurring verdict carry its own weight. The witnesses do not divide. Keil traces the counsel forward into the fatal war; Ellicott fixes the phrase as the chronicler's own comment; Wesley marks how the evil tutelage passed from father to kinsmen without a break. Between them they show that the young king was never for a moment without a corrupter at his elbow — first his father, then his mother's people — and that the counsel which flattered him was in truth conducting him, step by step, to his death.
5:
"He walked also after their counsel, and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead." The witnesses trace the first fruit of the evil counsel — a Judean king marching in a northern king's quarrel. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in "he walked in their counsel" an echo of Ps. 1:1, and reads the verse as Ahaziah becoming a close partner in the politics of his ally, joining his expedition against the Syrians — words, he notes, that are not in Kings. Where the parallel at 2 Kings 8:28 reads that he went "with" Joram, the chronicler writes that he went "against" Hazael, and adds the title "king of Israel" of his own hand; Hazael himself he ties to the earlier notices at 2 Kings 8:8 and 2 Kings 13:3. He lingers over a curiosity of the Hebrew: the word for "the Syrians" here is ha-rammim rather than the usual form, which the Septuagint took to mean "the archers," as if from the verb to shoot; perhaps, Ellicott suggests, the chronicler intended "the archers," comparing 1 Samuel 31:3 and Jeremiah 4:29.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain what the chronicler deliberately leaves out. He does not touch the conspiracy against Joram narrated in 2 Kings 9, at whose head stood Jehu, the captain of the host, whom God had caused to be anointed king over Israel by a young scholar of the prophets sent from Elisha, and whom he had called to root out the idolatrous family of Ahab — for it did not belong to the plan of the Chronicle to narrate that history. The reader of Chronicles is told only so much of Jehu as bears on the fate of the king of Judah.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke passes the reader to the fuller account at 2 Kings 8:28, and the reformed John Gill reads the verse as Ahaziah doing exactly as his counsellors advised, in matters of state no less than of religion. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Ellicott fixes the wording and its philological oddities; Keil marks what the chronicler suppresses and why; Clarke and Gill anchor the alliance to the parallel. Between them they show the snare closing: the king who took Ahab's house for his counsellors now takes Ahab's son for his comrade-in-arms, and rides north into the very campaign at whose end Jehu waits.
7:
"And the destruction of Ahaziah was of God by coming to Joram." The witnesses seize on that flat ascription of the king's ruin to God himself, and read the whole coincidence of the visit as the working of providence. The reformed John Gill puts it in the language of the divine decree: the destruction was of God's appointing, according to his purpose and counsel, brought about by an overruling providence that ordered the very occasion and manner of it, and ordered them justly, for the king's sins. Nothing here is accident; the timing itself is the judgment.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the striking noun the chronicler chooses. The word rendered "destruction" (tebusah, a being trodden down) occurs nowhere else in Scripture; under divine leading, they say, Ahaziah had come to Joram, there to find his death, and when he was come he went out with Joram against Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom God had anointed to extirpate the house of Ahab, as told at 2 Kings 9:1-10; where our verse reads "against Jehu," the parallel at 2 Kings 9:21 has the more vivid "to meet Jehu." It was thus in the very company of the doomed king, and marching against the very man God had raised up to be the executioner, that Ahaziah met his end — an end he walked into by the freest of his own choices, yet one that fell exactly where the divine sentence had appointed.

Charles Ellicott, his fellow grammatical-historical witness, renders the clause "from God came the downtreading of Ahaziah, so that he went to Joram," and marks the rare word as he does — tebusah found only here, akin to the mebusah of Isaiah 22:5. The coincidence of the visit with Jehu's rebellion, he says, revealed the working of divine providence, so that the three chief representatives of the house of Ahab — Joram, Jezebel, and Ahaziah — were caught up together in one catastrophe of ruin, while Athaliah alone escaped for the time. He fixes the genealogy too: "son of Nimshi" means grandson, Jehu being the son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi, and the LORD had anointed him according to 1 Kings 19:16. The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the decree, Keil and Ellicott fix the unique word and the providence it carries, and all three agree that Ahaziah's fall was no misfortune of war but a summons kept: the God who had marked Ahab's house for the sword drew the king of Judah, by a visit he chose freely, into the very hour of its execution.
8:
"When Jehu was executing judgment upon the house of Ahab, he found the princes of Judah and the sons of the brethren of Ahaziah, that ministered to Ahaziah, and slew them." The witnesses read the slaughter as part of one divinely directed sweep. The reformed John Gill sets it in its wider carnage: Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab — on Joram his son, and on seventy more, his kinsfolk, courtiers, and priests — and the Judean attendants of Ahaziah were caught in the same net.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the men were the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, in his train as his servants, and that the chronicler records the killing only as a proof of the divinely directed extirpation of every member of the idolatrous royal house; when and where Jehu met them he does not say, though 2 Kings 10:12-14 supplies the scene on the road as Jehu went up to Samaria to stamp out the worship of Baal. Charles Ellicott presses the force of "executing judgment," a Hebrew phrase that strictly means to plead with or argue a cause, as at 1 Samuel 12:7; when God is said to plead with men the notion of judicial punishment is commonly involved, as at Joel 3:2 and Isaiah 66:16, so that Jehu is an instrument of divine vengeance even while he serves his own ambition, exactly as the savage Assyrian conqueror does in Isaiah 10:5-7.

Over the identity of the slain a real dispute surfaces. Ellicott takes the "brethren" of 2 Kings 10:12-14, forty-two in number, as kinsmen in the wide sense — nephews, cousins, and grandsons of the king — the princes of Judah being members of the court in charge of them, perhaps counted within that forty-two. Against this he sets the critic Thenius, who argued that they must be Ahaziah's own literal brothers, whom the chronicler had conveniently "got rid of" on an earlier occasion at 2 Chron. 21:17 and v.1, because he wanted a divine judgment already in Jehoram's lifetime. Such arbitrary criticism, Ellicott answers, hardly deserves refutation, resting as it does on the untenable assumption that Jehoram could have begotten no children before Ahaziah, whom he begot in his eighteenth or nineteenth year. The witnesses do not divide among themselves: Gill and Keil fix the fact and its theological point, Ellicott the grammar and the geography, and all read the killing as one more stroke in the God-appointed felling of Ahab's whole connexion — Judah's princes falling with Israel's because they had made themselves the retinue of an apostate king.
9:
"And he sought Ahaziah, and they caught him (for he was hid in Samaria), and brought him to Jehu; and when they had slain him, they buried him." The witnesses attend both to the manner of the death and to the reason given for the burial. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Ahaziah had fled when Joram was wounded by Jehu, and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds that, though himself wounded, he had made his escape, pointing to 2 Kings 9:27.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe Jehu's men catching the king as he hid in Samaria, bringing him to Jehu, and slaying him; then his own servants buried him, saying, "He is a son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart." They observe that 2 Kings 9:27 gives more exact information — Ahaziah overtaken near Jibleam in his flight, wounded, fleeing to Megiddo and dying there, then carried by his servants to Jerusalem and buried with his fathers in the city of David — and they hold the two records to be reconciled, referring the reader to their fuller discussion there. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way, pointing to the different account at 2 Kings 9:27 as one to be harmonized with this.

Charles Ellicott takes the divergence differently, and here the witnesses openly part. He sets out the tradition of 2 Kings 9:27-28 in full — Ahaziah fleeing by the way of the garden house, smitten at the ascent of Gur beside Ibleam, dying at Megiddo, and buried in his own grave with his fathers in the city of David — and welcomes the difference rather than smoothing it away: "such divergences are valuable," he says, "because they help to establish the independence of the two accounts." The chronicler's own hand he finds throughout: the note that Ahaziah was buried for the sake of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD, is a didactic remark in his usual manner, and the closing clause — that the house of Ahaziah had none left with strength to hold the kingdom — is again his own style, forming the transition to Athaliah's usurpation, as at 2 Chron. 13:20. So the debate is a real one of method: whether the two death-accounts are a single event to be reconciled, as Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke hold, or two independent traditions whose very unlikeness is their worth, as Ellicott judges. What none disputes is the chronicler's point — that even this apostate grandson of a godly king was granted a decent grave for his grandfather's piety, so that the memory of the just proved a blessing to a descendant who had done nothing to earn it.
10:
"But when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah." The witnesses read the atrocity as the last and boldest stroke of Ahab's house, now reaching for the throne of David itself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that after her son's death Athaliah ascended the throne and had all the male members of the royal house murdered, only the infant Joash, a year old, being rescued with his nurse by the princess Jehoshabeath; the same narrative, in nearly the same words, stands at 2 Kings 11:1-3. Charles Ellicott adds a textual note: for "destroyed," read with Kings, the versions, and some Hebrew manuscripts, the received Hebrew has a scribe's slip meaning "she spake"; and "all the seed royal," he observes, must include, beyond Ahaziah's own offspring, the many persons more or less nearly connected with the royal family who would still have been left even after the massacres of v.1 and v.8.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scene as a duel of two women over the covenant. Here is a wicked woman labouring to destroy the house of David that she might set up a throne for herself upon its ruins; Athaliah cut off all the seed royal, perhaps meaning to transmit the crown of Judah to some of her own relations, so that though her family had been cut off in Israel by Jehu it might yet be planted in Judah. And over against her, in the verse to come, stands a good woman preserving the line, that a lamp might be ordained for God's anointed — for no word of God shall fall to the ground.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out what hung in the balance. Nothing but the miraculous intervention of divine providence, he says, could have saved the line of David at this hour and preserved the prophecy of the Messiah; the whole truth of that prophecy, and the salvation of the world, seemed now suspended on the brittle thread of the life of a single infant a year old, whose age he fixes from 2 Chron. 24:1 — and to destroy that child was the very interest of the reigning power. But God can save by few as well as by many; he had purposed, and vain were all the counter-exertions of earth and hell. The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott secure the fact and the text; Henry frames the wicked woman's ambition; Clarke measures the Messianic stakes. Between them they show the promise to David hanging by a hair over a cradle, and a usurping queen unable, for all her slaughter, to cut the one thread that God had resolved to keep whole.
11:
"But Jehoshabeath the daughter of the king took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons that were slain, and put him and his nurse in a bedchamber." The witnesses gather round the woman whose single act of courage saved the covenant line. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify her exactly: Jehoshabeath, daughter of king Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, was the sister of Ahaziah, and she hid the child from Athaliah so that she slew him not. Charles Ellicott adds the philology and the parallels. The name, "Jehoshabeath," is the "Jehosheba" of Kings, of the same form as "Elisheba" at Exodus 6:23 and the "Elisabeth" of Luke 1:7; "that were slain" is more precisely "that were to be put to death," the child snatched from among his doomed kinsmen before the blow fell; and the "bedchamber" is literally a chamber of beds, the room where the bedding was stored, as he explains at 2 Kings 11:2.

Over one detail a genuine dispute arises — whether Jehoshabeath was indeed the wife of the high priest, and the child hidden within the temple precinct. Ellicott affirms it with Josephus, and against the critic Thenius, who doubted the fact on two grounds: that the high priest did not live in the temple, and that the chronicler contradicts himself in lodging a priest's wife within the sacred courts. Both objections Ellicott sets aside as resting on irrelevant proof-texts, and he cites Ewald, who called the statement "genuinely historical"; there is, he concludes, not the smallest reason to doubt it. So the marriage of the princess to the priest is left standing — and with it the very link, royal and priestly at once, by which the rescue could be carried through and the child concealed in the house of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the deed. Over against the wicked woman who would extirpate the house of David stands here a good woman effectually preserving it: one of the late king's sons, a child of a year old, was rescued from among the dead and saved alive by the care of Jehoiada's wife, that a lamp might be ordained for God's anointed. The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the woman, the name, and the manner of the rescue, and defend its historicity; Henry names its meaning. Between them they show how the whole future of the promise turned on the nerve of one princess, sister to the dead king and wife to the living priest, who dared to carry a royal infant out of a massacre and hide him where a queen's malice could not reach.
12:
"And he was with them hid in the house of God six years; and Athaliah reigned over the land." The chapter ends on the strange, quiet safety of a hidden child while a usurper holds the throne, and the witnesses read the sanctuary as both refuge and pledge. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the hiding-place with the Targum: the child was concealed in "the house of the sanctuary of God," or, as he had said on the previous verse, in the holy of holies itself — the one place to which Athaliah, for all her power, had no access, so that there Joash lay hidden with his affectionate aunt through the whole of her reign. The temple that the house of Ahab had laboured to eclipse now shelters the heir it had tried to destroy.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to a small variant in the opening words. "He was with them hid" means with Jehoiada and his wife, the priest and princess who had rescued him; where our text reads "with them," Kings has "with her," the Septuagint "with him," and the Syriac and Arabic again "with her," a difference he ties to his note on 2 Kings 11:3. His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch reads the verse plainly for its two facts held in tension: the child was hidden in the house of God six full years, and all that while Athaliah reigned over the land — the true king an infant in the temple, the false queen on the throne, and the whole future of David's line waiting out the usurpation in concealment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology to which the whole chapter has been tending. That the child was preserved through these six years was so that a lamp might be ordained for God's anointed; for no word of God shall fall to the ground, and the whole truth of the prophecies that the Messiah should come from David — and with him the salvation of the world — had seemed to hang upon the brittle thread of a single infant's life, to destroy whom was the very interest of the reigning power; but God had purposed, and vain were the efforts of earth and hell. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke fixes the sanctuary refuge, Ellicott the textual detail of his keepers, Keil the six years set against Athaliah's reign, and Henry the promise those years preserved. Between them they close the account of a bloody usurpation on a note of hidden hope: the lamp of David is not out but only covered, kept burning in the house of God against the day, six years off, when a priest will bring the child forth and the throne will be given back to the line the LORD had sworn to keep.
6:
Wounded at Ramah, Joram withdraws to Jezreel to be healed, and Ahaziah goes down to see his sick ally — the visit that will prove fatal. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott works carefully over the verse's tangled text. "And he returned" is Joram, not Ahaziah; the Hebrew "because the wounds" makes no sense and should read "of the wounds," with Kings, the Septuagint, the Syriac, Arabic, and Targum, the particle for "because" having grown out of the little word for "from." The rare term for "wounds" (makkim) occurs elsewhere only at 2 Kings 8:29 and 2 Kings 9:15. Whether Ahaziah "went down" from Ramah or from Jerusalem, Ellicott says, is not clear, and he points to 2 Kings 9:14; and the ally's name, spelled "Jehoram" here, is the "Joram" of Kings and the versions.

The knottiest point is the name of the Judean king himself, who appears in this verse as "Azariah." Ellicott judges it a simple scribal mistake for "Ahaziah," the reading of Kings, the Septuagint, the Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic, and several Hebrew manuscripts — the same king who stands as Jehoahaz at 2 Chron. 21:17 and as Ahaziah at v.1. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, canvassing the survivor's cluster of names, was content rather to let all three stand as genuine names of one man; so the reader meets a real divergence — whether "Azariah" is a copyist's slip to be mended against the versions, or one more authentic title of a king who bore several.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry look past the philology to the providence in the visit. Keil reads Joram's return to Jezreel to be healed, and Ahaziah's going down to see him because he was sick, as the innocent-seeming step that God would use for judgment: it is the coming-to-Joram that the next verse calls the destruction of Ahaziah. Henry says the same in his running comment — Ahaziah came on a visit to Joram just at the moment Jehu was executing the judgment of God upon that idolatrous house, and so was caught, as in a snare, and cut off with them. The witnesses do not divide over the sense of the scene. A king pays a courtesy call on a wounded kinsman and rides straight into the sword appointed for another dynasty; the text-critic's small corrections and the preacher's large lesson meet in the one fact that this journey, undertaken in friendship, was in truth the road to his death.
